Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette: As a train conductor, Ana was accustomed to being in control and ensuring the safety of her passengers. However, since childhood, she had struggled with the memories of witnessing domestic violence between her parents. The sound of loud noises, like the screeching of brakes or the yelling of angry voices, would send her heart racing and transport her back to those terrifying moments. When darkness fell, Ana felt a sense of unease wash over her. She would try to distract herself by focusing on her work, checking and rechecking the train's systems, but she couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked in every shadowy corner. Her mind would wander to the nights spent hiding under the bed as a child, listening to her parents' arguments escalate into violence. The memories felt so vivid, so real, that Ana often struggled to put them in chronological order - the sounds, sights, and even tastes (the metallic tang of blood) blended together in a jumbled mess. Ana's inability to stop those bad things from happening to her and others weighed heavily on her conscience. She couldn't help but wonder what she could have done differently, how life would have been different if only... The 'what ifs' swirled in her head like a maelstrom, drawing her down into the depths of self-blame and recrimination. Her mind told her that she was responsible for not protecting her loved ones, that it was all her fault. As Ana navigated her daily routine, these negative appraisals crept into every aspect of her life. She found herself perpetually on edge, checking doors and locks multiple times, as if the mere act could ward off potential danger. At night, she would lie awake, listening for any unexpected sounds that might signal an intruder or a threat. When her heart started racing, she knew it was only a matter of time before the memories came flooding back - and with them, the crushing sense of helplessness. Ana tried to cope by throwing herself into work, volunteering for extra shifts and pushing herself to exhaustion. She would also engage in counterfactual thinking, imagining alternative scenarios where her parents' arguments had ended differently. However, these strategies offered only temporary respite. When she was alone with her thoughts, the memories came flooding back - more vivid than ever. Ana's attempts at coping took a toll on her physical health as well. She began restricting food, eating less and less in an attempt to feel some semblance of control over her body. Her relationships suffered too; friends and family grew concerned about her increasingly withdrawn nature. Yet Ana couldn't shake off the feeling that she was living on borrowed time - one misstep away from disaster. As the months dragged on, Ana's world shrunk further and further. She stopped socializing, afraid of being in situations where loud noises or dark spaces might trigger another episode. The cycle tightened: memories triggered fear, which in turn fed her negative appraisals, propelling her into a vortex of maladaptive coping mechanisms. By the time she sought help, Ana was convinced that she would never be able to break free from this toxic loop - and that she would forever be trapped in the darkness of her own making. Ana's eyes locked onto hers as she recounted the litany of symptoms that had become her daily reality. The weight of those experiences hung heavy on her shoulders, a constant reminder of what she'd endured - and the terror she still carried within.
